definition: Amazon Lex is a service for building conversational interfaces into any application using voice and text.
details: It powers the Amazon Alexa virtual assistant. In April 2017, the platform was released to the developer community, and suggested that it could be used for conversational interfaces (chatbots or otherwise) including Web, mobile apps, robots, toys, drones, and more. Amazon already had launched Alexa Voice Services, which developers can use to integrate Alexa into their own devices, like smart speakers, alarm clocks, etc.; however, Lex will not require that end users interact with the Alexa assistant per se, but rather any type of assistant or interface. As of February 2018, users can now define a response for Amazon Lex chatbots directly from the AWS management console.

explainer.lead: Amazon Lex is an AWS service for adding voice and text conversations to applications. Developers can use it to build chatbots and other assistants without requiring users to interact with Alexa.

tiers.eli5: Amazon Lex is like a kit for building a helpful receptionist inside an app. A person can speak or type to it, and the app can answer through the assistant its developer designed.
tiers.practitioner: Developers configure a Lex bot and connect it to an application that supplies voice or text input and presents the response. Responses can be defined through the AWS management console; Lex V2, released in 2021, provides a revised console and V2 APIs. V2 supports multiple languages in one bot, managed as a single resource, and Lex should not be confused with Alexa Voice Services, which integrates Alexa itself into devices.
tiers.paperLevel: Amazon Lex is a service for constructing application-hosted conversational interfaces over voice and text inputs, with developer-defined responses returned through the bot. Amazon released it to developers in April 2017 and released Lex V2 in 2021. V2 represents multiple languages within one bot as a single managed resource; Lex does not require end users to interact with the Alexa assistant.

explainer.example: In a mobile library app, a user types, “What time does the library close?” The app passes the message to its Lex bot, which returns the configured answer, “The library closes at 6 p.m.,” for the app to display.

usedIn.name: Amazon Alexa
usedIn.detail: Lex powers the Alexa virtual assistant.

usedIn.name: Web and mobile applications
usedIn.detail: Developers can embed Lex-based chatbots and other conversational interfaces.

usedIn.name: Robots, toys, and drones
usedIn.detail: Amazon identified these as possible hosts for Lex-powered conversational interfaces.

explainer.intuition: Lex provides the conversational layer between a person and an application. The application handles the surrounding experience, while the developer designs the assistant and its responses rather than having to present Alexa as the interface.
howItWorks: A developer creates a conversational bot with Amazon Lex.
The developer defines responses, including directly through the AWS management console.
An application sends the user's voice or text input to the bot.
The bot supplies a response for the application to present to the user.
explainer.whyItMatters: Lex lets developers add voice and text conversations to applications ranging from websites and mobile apps to robots and toys. It also gives them freedom to create their own assistant or interface instead of requiring users to interact with Alexa.
misconceptions: Using Lex does not mean end users must interact with Alexa.
Lex is not Alexa Voice Services: the latter integrates Alexa into devices, while Lex supports many kinds of assistants and interfaces.
In Lex V2, multiple languages do not have to be managed as separate bot resources; they can belong to one bot.
